name: Kaingang
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 1 refine it). One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Jolkesky 2009.
sweep_summary: Kaingang (kain1272) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant, final (final stress), deciding quote from Jolkesky 2009 p. 682. The single title-works with stress in the title, Wetzels 2010 'Word prosody and the distribution of oral/nasal contour consonants in Kaingang' (Brill, DOI 10.1163/9789047427087_015), is clearly about Kaingang word prosody but remains unread: it is paywalled ($40), the Brill landing page (live and the Internet Archive 2020) carries no abstract or preview text, and OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, CORE, HathiTrust, archive.org, BASE, the VU portal, academia.edu, Google Books and the Curt Nimuendajú digital library all yielded no open copy; it stays the top acquisition target (high). Note the pagination discrepancy: Brill and Crossref give pp. 253-270, Glottolog 235-252. A related open Wetzels paper (Alfa 2008, nasal contours) was downloaded and is silent on stress; Wetzels & Meira 2010 'A survey of South American stress systems' (De Gruyter, closed) is a medium-priority lead. Everything readable held by the project agrees with the classification: Cavalcante 1987 (pp. 13-14, 34) states an explicit rule — intensity accent on the last phonological syllable of content words, particles and pronouns unstressed, identical for São Paulo and Paraná dialects; Jolkesky 2009 (p. 682, 684) gives predictable final stress for Cacique Doble; Teixeira 1988 (pp. 37-38) shows the only final unstressed syllables in Nonoai are non-phonemic echo vowels; D'Angelis 1998 relays Wiesemann 1964 that the echo vowel never bears word stress. Recommendation: keep fixed-dominant final; promote Cavalcante 1987 pp. 13-14 to deciding source (dissertation, two dialects, explicit rule and domain) with Jolkesky 2009 as corroboration; fix the catalog's SETA URL (correct article id 557/474, not 559/460, which is a literature paper); set domain = content word with particles/pronouns excluded. new_statements.quote: Dentro de cada um dos dois conjuntos de palavras acima a ocorrência e a não ocorrência do acento de intensidade são inteiramente predizíveis: no conjunto (a) ocorre o acento de intensidade sistematicamente na última sílaba fonológica; no conjunto (b) não ocorre acento de intensidade. A seguinte regra dará conta de sua colocação. R.3, colocação de acento de intensidade: [...] (uma vogal torna-se tônica quando situada na última sílaba de uma palavra principal).
new_statements.translation: Within each of the two word sets above, the occurrence and non-occurrence of intensity accent are entirely predictable: in set (a) [content words: nouns, descriptives, verbs] the intensity accent occurs systematically on the last phonological syllable; in set (b) [particles and pronouns] no intensity accent occurs. The following rule accounts for its placement. R.3, placement of intensity accent: [...] (a vowel becomes tonic when located in the last syllable of a main word).

new_statements.reading: Fixed final stress on content words in both the São Paulo and Paraná dialects, with particles and pronouns unstressed — i.e. fixed-dominant, final (final stress), domain = the content word, clitic-like function words excluded. Agrees with Jolkesky 2009 (Cacique Doble, RS) and Teixeira 1988 (Nonoai), so three independent dialect descriptions coincide. Read from the scanned of a scanned typescript; the scanned text has minor character errors but the rule statement is unambiguous.

tone_statements.citation: Nascimento, Márcia; Marcus Maia; Letícia Rebollo Couto. 2016. Tempo e evidencialidade na língua Kaingang – uma abordagem experimental. Letras de Hoje 51(3): 402-411. Porto Alegre: PUCRS. DOI 10.15448/1984-7726.2016.3.22543.
tone_statements.quote: No primeiro experimento, identificamos um processo suprassegmental atuante sobre a categoria de Tempo nesta língua. Em verbos finalizados por segmentos consonantais, a prosódia opera como traço distintivo de passado e futuro, tanto em enunciados assertivos, quanto em interrogativos. Através desse experimento e também de análises acústicas, mostramos que a língua Kaingang, conhecida como uma língua acentual, apresenta tom gramatical atuando na categoria de tempo.
tone_statements.translation: In the first experiment we identified a suprasegmental process acting on the category of Tense in this language. In verbs ending in consonantal segments, prosody operates as the distinctive feature of past and future, in declarative as well as interrogative utterances. Through this experiment and also through acoustic analyses we show that Kaingang, known as an accentual language, has grammatical tone operating on the tense category.
tone_statements.locator: Resumo (abstract), article landing page DC.Description; pp. 402-411
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone; grammatical (verbal) tone restricted to tense marking on consonant-final verbs: high/rising pitch on the verb = future, low/falling = past; otherwise an accentual (final-stress) language.

tone_statements.citation: Nascimento, Márcia. 2013. Tempo, modo, aspecto e evidencialidade em Kaingang. Dissertação de Mestrado em Linguística, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Faculdade de Letras (orient. Marcus Maia & Letícia Rebollo Couto). xiv+127 pp. (Glottolog dates it 2012.)
tone_statements.quote: Estes resultados nos levam a considerar que a oposição de tons em Kaingang é funcional em alguns pontos específicos do sistema, neste caso para a oposição de passado (L*L%) e futuro (H*H%) no núcleo, mas também para a oposição assertiva e interrogativa no pré-núcleo ... Tais oposições tonais, numa língua que não pode ser classificada como tonal, nos leva a pensar na possibilidade da emergência de um sistema tonal ou no resquício de um sistema tonal, em termos de evolução da linguagem. Os resultados da análise acústica confirmam a oposição contrastante entre o acento nuclear passado L*L% e o acento nuclear futuro H*H%.
tone_statements.translation: These results lead us to consider that the opposition of tones in Kaingang is functional at some specific points of the system, here for the opposition of past (L*L%) and future (H*H%) in the nucleus, but also for the assertive vs interrogative opposition in the pre-nucleus ... Such tonal oppositions, in a language that cannot be classified as tonal, lead us to think of the possible emergence of a tonal system or of the residue of a tonal system, in terms of language evolution. The results of the acoustic analysis confirm the contrastive opposition between the past nuclear accent L*L% and the future nuclear accent H*H%.
tone_statements.summary: Says Kaingang is not a tone language, but consonant-final verbs mark past vs future by falling vs rising utterance-final F0 ('prosodic inflection'); perception test + Praat; upstep ¡H* on particle tỹ.

tone_statements.citation: Wiesemann, Ursula. 1964. Phonological syllables and words in Kaingáng. In H. Becher (ed.), Beiträge zur Völkerkunde Südamerikas: Festgabe für Herbert Baldus, 307-313. Hannover.
tone_statements.quote: Syllables are distributed into the phonological word, a unit that carries a single stress. A word may be simple or complex. 3.1. A simple word is characterized by one stressed syllable, as well as by initial and terminal phonological features which mark its boundaries. The placement of word stress is phonemically significant and its occurrence is an obligatory feature of the phonological word. Word stress indicates the peak of intensity in the word, and is accompanied by the lengthening of syllables as described in Section 2.4. [...] 3.1.1. In ordinary words the word stress is accompanied by the highest pitch in the word. The syllables preceding the stress ascend in pitch, while those following the stress descend in pitch. [...] 3.2. Complex words differ from simple words in that the latter [sic] have, in addition to their word stress, a 'suppressed stress', i.e., they contain an element which in isolation would have a word stress, but which in combination loses its word stress. This stress may be partially suppressed or completely suppressed. When the stress is only partially suppressed it marks a subpeak of intensity.

sources.note: Intensity accent falls systematically on the last phonological syllable of content words (nouns, descriptives, verbs); particles and pronouns are unstressed. Rule R.3: a vowel becomes tonic when in the last syllable of a 'palavra principal'. The same rule holds without change for Paraná Kaingang. Confirms the final-stress coding and refines the domain: word-level, content words only, clitic-like particles/pronouns outside the rule.

sources.citation: Teixeira, José Baltazar. 1988. Contribuição para a fonologia do dialeto Kaingáng de Nonoai. Dissertação de mestrado, IEL-UNICAMP, 49 pp. DOI 10.47749/t/unicamp.1988.51592
sources.quote: 'neste dialeto do Kaingáng, todas as sílabas átonas em final de palavra são constituídas por uma aproximante e uma vogal' and that vowel is a predictable echo of the preceding stressed vowel, so it is excluded from the phonological representation (e.g. [ˈgoyo] 'água' = /goy/). I.e. the only surface non-final stresses are echo-vowel words; stress is final over phonological syllables.
sources.note: The only word-final unstressed syllables in Nonoai Kaingang are predictable echo vowels after approximants, copying the stressed vowel of the preceding syllable, and are excluded from phonological representation — i.e. phonological words end in the stressed syllable.

sources.citation: Jolkesky, Marcelo Pinho de Valhery. 2009. Fonologia e prosódia do Kaingang falado em Cacique Doble. Anais do SETA 3: 675-685. Campinas: IEL-UNICAMP. (the Internet Archive 20200804, revistas.iel.unicamp.br seta/article/download/557/474)
sources.quote: 'O acento lexical em Kaingang é previsível, ocorrendo na última sílaba' (p.682); phonological word right-headed, 'o acento recai no pé mais à direita' with monosyllabic feet (p.684); ex. /nunũˈnɛ̃/ 'caracol', /peˈpo/ 'sapo', /kɹonˈkɹon/ 'beber pl.'
sources.note: Lexical stress is predictable and falls on the last syllable (Cacique Doble, RS variety); at the phonological-word level the rightmost foot carries prominence ('jâmbico reverso'), marked by an intensity peak.

sources.citation: D'Angelis, Wilmar da Rocha. 1998. Traços de modo e modos de traçar geometrias: línguas Macro-Jê & teoria fonológica. Tese de doutorado, Unicamp.
sources.quote: a vogal final nas seqüências à esquerda ... é fonética, porque sua qualidade é totalmente previsível e ela nunca porta o acento da palavra. Nas palavras de Wetzels (1995a:271), "as aproximantes /r,j,w/ desencadeiam uma regra de epêntese vocálica, que cria uma cópia da vogal nuclear subjacente da última sílaba".
sources.locator: text lines ~5249-5253 and ~5324-5326 of the (chapter on Kaingang syllable/nasal contours)
sources.note: No placement rule of its own; reports second-hand that the epenthetic final echo vowel 'never bears word stress' (citing Wiesemann 1964:309 and Wetzels 1995a:271) and that Wiesemann found word stress lengthens the stressed syllable. Consistent with final stress on the underlying last syllable.

The note-5 remark that the echo vowel of the reduplicated final syllable is unstressed is compatible with Cavalcante's formulation 'última sílaba fonológica' (the echo syllable being non-phonological/epenthetic in later analyses) but is not itself a placement statement. sources.citation: Nascimento, Márcia; Marcus Maia; Letícia Rebollo Couto. 2016. Tempo e evidencialidade na língua Kaingang – uma abordagem experimental. Letras de Hoje 51(3): 402-411. Porto Alegre: PUCRS. DOI 10.15448/1984-7726.2016.3.22543.
sources.quote: No primeiro experimento, identificamos um processo suprassegmental atuante sobre a categoria de Tempo nesta língua. Em verbos finalizados por segmentos consonantais, a prosódia opera como traço distintivo de passado e futuro, tanto em enunciados assertivos, quanto em interrogativos. Através desse experimento e também de análises acústicas, mostramos que a língua Kaingang, conhecida como uma língua acentual, apresenta tom gramatical atuando na categoria de tempo.

tone.translation: In the first experiment we identified a suprasegmental process acting on the category of Tense in this language. In verbs ending in consonantal segments, prosody operates as the distinctive feature of past and future, in declarative as well as interrogative utterances. Through this experiment and also through acoustic analyses we show that Kaingang, known as an accentual language, has grammatical tone operating on the tense category.
tone.summary: No lexical tone; grammatical (verbal) tone restricted to tense marking on consonant-final verbs: high/rising pitch on the verb = future, low/falling = past; otherwise an accentual (final-stress) language.
tone.says: Experiment 1 plus acoustic analysis show a suprasegmental process on Tense -- in consonant-final verbs prosody (pitch) is the distinctive feature of past vs future in declaratives and interrogatives; Kaingang, 'known as an accentual language', has grammatical tone operating on the tense category.

sources.citation: Nascimento, Márcia. 2013. Tempo, modo, aspecto e evidencialidade em Kaingang. Dissertação de Mestrado em Linguística, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Faculdade de Letras (orient. Marcus Maia & Letícia Rebollo Couto). xiv+127 pp. (Glottolog dates it 2012.)
sources.quote: Estes resultados nos levam a considerar que a oposição de tons em Kaingang é funcional em alguns pontos específicos do sistema, neste caso para a oposição de passado (L*L%) e futuro (H*H%) no núcleo, mas também para a oposição assertiva e interrogativa no pré-núcleo ... Tais oposições tonais, numa língua que não pode ser classificada como tonal, nos leva a pensar na possibilidade da emergência de um sistema tonal ou no resquício de um sistema tonal, em termos de evolução da linguagem. Os resultados da análise acústica confirmam a oposição contrastante entre o acento nuclear passado L*L% e o acento nuclear futuro H*H%.

tone.translation: These results lead us to consider that the opposition of tones in Kaingang is functional at some specific points of the system, here for the opposition of past (L*L%) and future (H*H%) in the nucleus, but also for the assertive vs interrogative opposition in the pre-nucleus ... Such tonal oppositions, in a language that cannot be classified as tonal, lead us to think of the possible emergence of a tonal system or of the residue of a tonal system, in terms of language evolution. The results of the acoustic analysis confirm the contrastive opposition between the past nuclear accent L*L% and the future nuclear accent H*H%.
